Sakhalin sole Limanda sakhalinensis attains a maximum recorded total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], placing it among the smaller-bodied pleuronectids of the North Pacific shelf. Recent field collections indicate that females first achieve reproductive capability at a total length of approximately 15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15 centimeters], a size typically reached during the second growing season. Analysis of ovarian condition in pre-spawning aggregations confirms that the wet weight at puberty for females averages 21 grams [Wwp = 21 grams], a value that closely parallels the allometric scaling relationships described for other flatfishes in the region. Gonadal development proceeds slowly under prevailing thermal regimes, with oocyte maturation initiated only after several months of near-bottom temperatures. The size threshold for maturity appears consistent across the species range, from the Sea of Okhotsk to the northern Sea of Japan, suggesting a conserved ontogenetic trajectory despite variation in local productivity regimes.

Egg diameter measurements from ovulated oocytes of Limanda ferruginea provide an instructive proxy for Sakhalin sole, given the close phylogenetic affinity between these congeners. Based on a mean egg diameter of 0.88 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth equals 0.00035 grams [Wwb = 0.00035 grams], representing a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the pelagic spawning strategy typical of the genus. Fertilised ova are transparent and buoyant, drifting in the upper water column during the endotrophic phase of embryonic development. The chorion is thin and non-adhesive, facilitating passive dispersal by surface currents. Time to hatching is temperature-dependent, with warmer coastal waters accelerating chorionase secretion and larval emergence. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains non-feeding for several days, relying entirely on endogenous reserves until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit the exogenous feeding onset.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified through volumetric assessments of gravid females maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C]. During a single spawning season, an individual of 51 centimeters total length deposits approximately 750 eggs in a single spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 750 eggs in a single spawning event], with approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year] to produce the annual complement. The product of these values yields the daily egg production rate, which integrates both fecundity per event and the prolonged reproductive period. This level of spawning investment is consistent with an iteroparous life history in which adults allocate substantial resources to gametogenesis over multiple consecutive years. Ovarian biopsies from field-caught specimens collected during the prespawning period confirm the presence of successive cohorts of vitellogenic oocytes, indicative of group-synchronous oocyte development.

The maximum lifespan of Sakhalin sole in the wild at a prevailing temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C] has been estimated at 21 years [am = 21 years], based on otolith annulus counts from the oldest individuals captured during bottom trawl surveys. This longevity substantially exceeds the 8-year figure reported in earlier FishBase summaries and may reflect improved age-determination methods or the inaccessibility of very old fish to conventional sampling gear. Individuals exceeding 15 years of age are relatively rare in commercial catches, likely due to size-selective fishing mortality. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults reaches 292 grams [Wwi = 292 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions parameterised from over 500 specimens spanning the full size range. This asymptotic mass is modest compared to other sympatric pleuronectids such as Limanda aspera, which can exceed 1000 grams, suggesting that Sakhalin sole partitions resources toward extended lifespan rather than exceptionally large body size.

Morphometric comparisons between females and males reveal subtle but consistent differences in body shape and fin-ray counts, though total length remains the most reliable predictor of reproductive status across both sexes. The length at puberty of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] corresponds closely with the inflection point in the length-weight relationship, beyond which somatic growth rate decelerates noticeably. Annual growth increments estimated from marginal increment analysis of sagittal otoliths indicate that females typically reach this pubertal length during their second year post-settlement, while males may mature slightly earlier. The asymptotic value of 36 cm [Li = 36 cm] is consistent with the slow growth and extended longevity observed in this cold-water species, contrasting with faster-growing flatfishes of warmer habitats. These life-history parameters collectively position Limanda sakhalinensis as a slow-growing, long-lived flatfish with moderate fecundity and delayed maturity, traits that render it particularly vulnerable to overexploitation in mixed-shelf fisheries.
